transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-29 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Ramos (Redwood SE), Sofia Patel (Arbor Head of ML), Liam O'Connor (Arbor Eng Manager), Noah Li (Arbor Security)

Auto Summary (auto-gen, may be rough):
Redwood walked through JSON mode for typed outputs, schema validations, and runtime tool calling patterns. Focus on guardrails for production (fallback models, typed errors), Console walkthrough for tracing/rollouts, and Optimize suggestions for batching/quantization. Customer asked about private deployment and audit logs. Next steps agreed for pilot SOW and security docs.

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone thanks for taking the time, I'm Maya from Redwood, this is Diego our SE. How are you all?
[00:08] Sofia: Hi Maya, thanks. Good, excited to see the JSON guardrail flow — we've been prototyping a bit but want to make outputs reliable.
[00:14] Diego: Great, we'll start with a quick overview then jump into Console and a live demo of JSON mode with a schema and a tool call example. I'll try to be concrete with latency numbers for your enrichment pipeline.
[00:22] Liam: Awesome. Quick ask — we care about latency for streaming enrichment and also need to understand cost implications.
[00:27] Noah: And security — SSO, KMS, audit logs, data residency. We'll need SOC2 material as well.
[00:33] Maya: Totally. We'll cover the private/VPC options and what goes in the security pack. Diego, can you start the demo?
[00:39] Diego: Yep. So JSON mode is our typed-output flow — you provide a JSON schema, runtime enforces structure and can auto-fallback to a sanitized error object if the model deviates. Here's an example: enrichment schema for product attributes, nested arrays — common for your inventory.
[01:02] Diego: (shares screen) Ok, here's the Console. On the left you see Models -> we have curated family entries. For the demo I'm using a low-latency 8k context important for your long descriptions. In this run we show schema validation in the request pipeline, also a tool binding to a tiny internal lookup service.
[01:25] Sofia: Is that the one that hits your KV cache? We've seen "K V cash" in earlier notes // little transcription error — but yes how's KV caching handled for repeated prefixes?
[01:34] Diego: Good call. We do prefix KV caching to speed up multi-token generation and maintain the KV store in GPU memory where possible. For repeated prefixes across calls, the runtime can reuse cached hidden states — the Console shows cache hit rate per route.
[01:47] Liam: What about batching? Our throughput is spiky.
[01:50] Diego: Redwood Optimize suggests batch sizes based on latency SLO. For example, if you target 200ms p95, we recommend small continuous batches (2–4) with cold-start policies for bursts. Optimize will run workload profiling and show the expected token cost delta — usually 10–30% improvement for typical enrichment workloads.
[02:12] Noah: Quick security detail — if we go Private VPC do we still get audit logs shipped to our SIEM?
[02:17] Maya: Yes, Private includes the control plane in your VPC; audit logs, structured trace exports and KMS/HSM integration are supported. We'll attach SOC2 docs.
[02:26] Sofia: Can you show a tool/function call where the model returns a typed action, like "call-enrich-service" with parameters?
[02:32] Diego: Sure. Live demo: schema defines an action object: {"action":"call_enrich","params":{"sku":string,"fields":[string]}}. The model can either return that action or raw text; in the runtime we enforce an action contract and if it's not adhered to we either coerce or return a structured error depending on your policy.
[02:56] (Diego runs example)
[03:01] Diego: You can see the model produced a valid action, the runtime then routed to the bound tool — that's hooked to a small microservice we use for demo. The Console shows the tool invocation trace with timings: model generation 78ms, invocation 22ms, total 100ms.
[03:18] Sofia: Nice. If the model hallucinates an unknown field, can we reject?
[03:22] Diego: Yes. Policies are configurable. You can set strict reject, coerce (map unknowns to null), or fallback to a simpler but higher-latency model. For production we usually recommend strict schema validation with a fallback that returns a typed error object to the caller.
[03:37] Liam: About fallbacks—if we fallback to a smaller model during peak, what's the typical quality delta and cost savings?
[03:44] Diego: Roughly, smaller quantized models can cut per-token cost by 40–60% with a modest quality drop. We use A/B evaluation sets you provide and Redwood Optimize recommends which model variants to route to during different load/cost windows.
[03:59] Maya: I'll add that the runtime supports handshake routing: route by cost or latency, and can fallback regionally. This helps keep the app online if a capacity zone is degraded.
[04:10] Noah: On compliance, do you have an artifact that maps Redwood features to our controls (ISO, SOC2, SAML)?
[04:16] Maya: Yes, we have a security pack; I'll upload a zip to the shared drive with SOC2 scope, SAML/SSO integration docs and KMS notes.
[04:24] Sofia: Can we look at an example where the model must output a list of normalized categories (strict enum) and also call a tool when confidence is low?
[04:32] Diego: Yup. Demo 2: schema with enum for categories, plus a confidence field. We can configure a policy: if confidence < 0.7 then emit an action "escalate_for_human". The runtime can also call a rewriter tool to try to sanitize and re-run the model automatically.
[04:52] (Diego triggers the low-confidence path)
[04:57] Diego: You can see the rerun attempt in the trace, Console shows two model calls and the rewriter tool invocation, final output is a typed error object flagged for human review.
[05:11] Liam: Does the Console surface token-level cost per call so we can correlate with queries?
[05:15] Diego: Yes, there's token and cost breakdown per request and per route. You can also filter by model variant, time window, and prompt set. That ties directly into cost reports in Optimize.
[05:25] Sofia: For the pilot we want to measure both latency and value — e.g., percent of correct category assignments that pass schema without human touch. Can Optimize help with that?
[05:35] Diego: Optimize integrates with your eval sets. You can feed ground-truth labels and it will run regression tests across model variants and quantization profiles. You get alerts for quality drift tied to prompt sets.
[05:46] Maya: Also, Optimize can recommend quantization profiles per workload; for example, for dense embedding tasks vs structured-output tasks you might pick different quant tapes.
[05:55] Noah: Sorry, "quant tapes"?
[05:57] Diego: (laughs) bad speech — I meant quantization profiles.
[06:00] Sofia: Ha. Notes the transcript will have a couple of those.
[06:05] Diego: Back to policies — CIR (canary/incremental rollout) is possible: you can route a small percentage of calls to a new model variant and measure schema pass rates & latency, then widen.
[06:17] Liam: That helps us avoid regressions. Who usually owns the rollout rules?
[06:21] Maya: The platform and your SRE collaborate; Redwood can operate the Dedicated or Private infra, or you can self-manage the runtime in your VPC with our control plane.
[06:30] Noah: For private on-prem we need HSM-backed keys — do you support HSM?
[06:34] Maya: Yes, HSM/KMS integrations are supported in Private. We'll include the HSM integration guide in the security pack.
[06:41] Sofia: Could you show the Console trace where a schema validation failure is correlated to a prompt set? We want to triage quickly.
[06:48] Diego: Sure. (shares screen) See this run: response failed schema because the model appended free text. You can click the request and see the prompt hash, the model config, and the eval comparison. We also surface suggested prompt adjustments and an example auto-fix via the rewriter tool.
[07:12] Liam: That auto-fix — is it another model call? Any cycle concerns?
[07:16] Diego: It's typically a short rewriter invocation — small model, few tokens, so it's cheap. We limit rewriter retries to avoid loops.
[07:25] Sofia: If we have a live product, will we be able to push a schema update safely?
[07:29] Diego: The Console has schema versioning and staged rollouts: create schema v2, run canary on 1% of traffic, collect metrics, then promote. All changes are auditable.
[07:40] Noah: On the audit trail, can we push logs to our SIEM and keep them for 12 months?
[07:45] Maya: Retention is configurable; for Private deployments you control the storage and retention policies. For Hosted, we have enterprise add-on retention plans.
[07:56] (brief pause while Diego loads a benchmark sheet)
[08:02] Diego: I brought a quick benchmark that approximates your enrichment workload: average prompt 250 tokens, 3–5 fields returned. On our Dedicated 8xA10g pool, typical p95 is ~180–220ms depending on batching. With continuous batching and KV cache we see a ~25% cost reduction in steady state.
[08:28] Liam: Can we run a short pilot with our sample data to validate these numbers?
[08:33] Maya: Absolutely. Pilot structure: 2 weeks, small reserved capacity, run your prompt set, gather metrics, and then we post a recommendation. We'll put numbers in the SOW.
[08:44] Sofia: For the pilot do you need production data or redacted samples?
[08:48] Diego: Redacted samples are fine for initial runs. For full security validation we'd use Private with your VPC and keys.
[08:57] Noah: Any gotchas around PII in the logs?
[09:00] Maya: We can mask PII at the ingestion layer and redact logs before they leave your VPC for further analysis.
[09:07] Sofia: Walk me through a full failure mode — model returns invalid JSON, runtime tries coercion, still fails, then what?
[09:14] Diego: Sequence: 1) first attempt fails schema, 2) runtime applies rewriter (small model) to sanitize, 3) if still fails, it returns typed error with failure code, 4) based on policy you can either surface to user or route to a human queue. All steps appear in trace.
[09:34] Liam: Do you support function-calling semantics where the LLM returns the exact function name and typed arguments and the runtime enforces call signatures?
[09:41] Diego: Yes, that's the core of JSON mode — typed actions with enforced signatures. We call them action contracts. You can map contract actions to HTTP/webhook tool integrations or internal services.
[09:51] Sofia: For mapping to our enrichment microservice, can we provide a swagger/openapi binding so the runtime validates against that?
[09:58] Diego: We have an OpenAPI-to-contract helper in Console. It can generate schemas and tool bindings. It's not perfect for every edge case but it accelerates onboarding.
[10:08] Noah: On permissions — can we set RBAC so only certain teams can change schema or rollout rules?
[10:13] Maya: Yes, Console supports RBAC and SSO integration; we'll show roles and what they can edit.
[10:19] Sofia: Any example of a customer who used typed outputs and reduced human review by X%?
[10:24] Diego: A customer in retail reported a 42% reduction in manual QA after moving to strict schema validation plus a rewriter for low-confidence cases. We anonymize clients in case studies but we can provide a redacted playbook.
[10:40] Liam: Can we backfill older results if schema changes? Say we change enums and need to reprocess last month's outputs.
[10:47] Diego: You can re-run batched inference jobs through Redwood's batch runner; Optimize helps forecast cost. For large backfills we'd recommend a dedicated job with isolated capacity.
[10:58] Sofia: Walk me through the instrumentation — if we want a custom metric like "schema_pass_rate_by_sku_category" can we emit that?
[11:05] Diego: Yes, the SDK and Console allow custom metrics that you can forward to your Prometheus/Grafana. We also export time-series for Optimize to analyze.
[11:15] (15 minute mark — discussion continues at higher level)
[11:48] Maya: Quick recap — pilot SOW, security pack, sample prompt set, and SE deep-dive. Any final security Qs?
[11:54] Noah: Just one: we need assurance on data exfil — what's your posture?
[11:58] Maya: For Private we run the control plane in your network, for Hosted we provide data contracts and strict retention + encryption. We'll map specifics in the security pack.
[12:10] Sofia: Ok. One more thing — can Optimize suggest quantization that maintains our structured output quality? Some quant methods hurt discrete token accuracy.
[12:19] Diego: Good point. Optimize runs targeted evals for structured tasks and flags quant profiles that degrade enum accuracy. We can lock profiles for structured outputs while quantizing only other workloads.
[12:32] Liam: That would be ideal.
[12:34] Maya: We'll include a recommended quantization matrix in the pilot deliverable.
[12:40] (closing 4–5 minutes, assign owners)
[12:45] Maya: Next steps: I'll send SOW + pricing, security pack. Diego will prep KV-cache notes and a short benchmark tailored to your sample prompts. Sofia to send sample prompt set. We aim to kick off week of 2026-05-04.
[12:59] Sofia: Thank you both — excited to try this out.
[13:02] Diego: Thanks everyone.
[13:05] (call ends)

Notes on transcript quality: speaker labels occasionally generic, minor transcription errors ("quant tapes" etc.). References shared: Demo deck (link posted in chat), Benchmark sheet (Google Sheet link), Security pack (to be uploaded).
